articles.title_orig: Five QB trades the Giants could make with Jaxson Dart out for season, including two with ties to John Harbaugh
articles.title_zh: Five QB trades the Giants could make with Jaxson Dart out for season, including two with ties to John Harbaugh
articles.content_orig:
The NFL season hasn't even hit Week 3, and the New York Giants are already in trouble. Jaxson Dart is out for the season after suffering a knee injury during the first quarter of New York's 28-6 loss to the Rams in Week 2.
With Dart out, the Giants turn the offense over to Jameis Winston. The former No. 1 overall pick just signed a two-year, $13 million extension with New York, so the Giants clearly have some faith in him, but if he struggles over the next week or two, that could open the door for John Harbaugh and general manager Joe Schoen to start poking around for another quarterback.
One potential problem with Winston is that he has a completely different skill set than Dart, which is why it wouldn't be completely crazy for the Giants to look around for a mobile QB.
With that in mind, we're going to take a look at five trade options that could make sense. This list will consist of two types of quarterbacks: guys who are mobile and/or guys who have ties to the coaching staff, which will make it much easier to get them acclimated to New York's offense.
If the Giants do end up making a trade, adding Huntley would probably make the most sense. Huntley spent the first four seasons of his career in Baltimore playing under Harbaugh. After heading to Miami in 2024, he returned to Baltimore last season to spend one more year with Harbaugh. During his time in Baltimore, Huntley saw plenty of action: He started a total of 12 games under Harbaugh, including a wild-card playoff game in January 2023.
The former Pro Bowler has the mobility Harbaugh loves to see in his quarterbacks, and he's always done a good job of using it on the field. One other upside to adding Huntley is that Greg Roman is on the Giants' coaching staff. Roman was the Ravens' offense coordinator during Huntlery's first three seasons, so he could quickly get him up to speed on the playbook that offensive coordinator Matt Nagy is running in New York.
Due to Lamar Jackson's injury history, the Ravens might not be willing to part ways with Huntley, but Baltimore did keep rookie Joe Fagano on the roster, so it's certainly possible that they would think about making a deal at the right price.
When the 2026 offseason started, Fields was in New York with the Jets, so a deal here would send him back to the Big Apple. The Jets ended up trading him to the Chiefs in March, which was a move that made sense at the time. When the offseason started, the Chiefs weren't sure if Patrick Mahomes was going to be ready to play in Week 1, so they added Fields as an insurance policy. With Mahomes now back on the field and looking like himself through the first two weeks, the Chiefs might be willing to ship Fields off to New York. One reason Kansas City might be open to a trade is that they already have a potential backup QB on the roster in rookie Garrett Nussmeier.
One reason Harbaugh might be interested in adding Fields is that the Giants' offensive coordinator, Matt Nagy, is already familiar with him. Nagy coached during Fields' rookie year with the Bears in 2021.
Titans QB Mitchell Trubisky
If the Giants want someone who could come in and learn the offense quickly, Trubisky would make a lot of sense. The Titans backup QB started his career in Chicago in 2017 when the Bears selected him with the second overall pick in the NFL Draft. In 2018, Trubisky led the Bears to an 11-3 record and a playoff appearance and his coach that year just happens to be the same guy who is currently serving as the offensive coordinator with the Giants: Nagy.
Nagy and Trubisky spent three seasons together in Chicago, and they went 25-13 during that span. That doesn't sound possible, but it's true. The only thing that could throw a wrench into a possible deal for Trubisky is that he plays for the Titans, who the Giants happen to be playing this week. The Titans probably wouldn't want to make a deal until after the game, which could potentially work out well, because that would give the Giants an extra week to figure out if Jameis Winston is good enough to carry the offense.
Colts QB Anthony Richardson
This might be the perfect time for Indianapolis to unload Richardson, who made a trade request earlier this offseason. He did win the backup job in Indianapolis this year, but if the Colts decided to trade him to New York, they'd still have Riley Leonard to take over the No. 2 spot.
By trading him away, it would allow the Colts to get something in return for Richardson, who was the No. 4 overall pick in the 2023 NFL Draft. If they keep him on the roster, he'll likely be leaving in free agency at the end of the year, and they'll get nothing in return.
This would almost be an ideal situation for both sides. Since the Colts didn't pick up Richardson's fifth-year option, that means his rookie deal is going to expire at the end of the 2026 season. If Richardson got dealt to New York and played well, that would put him in a position to cash in when he hits free agency after the season. As for the Giants, they wouldn't be tied to Richardson in any way, since his contract would expire at the end of the year.
If there's one guy in the NFL who can show up and be productive right away, it's definitely Flacco. Last season, he got traded to the Bengals on Oct. 7, didn't participate in his first practice until Oct. 8, but that didn't stop him from throwing for 219 yards and two touchdowns in a 27-18 loss to the Packers on Oct. 12.
The difference between Cincinnati and New York is that Flacco wouldn't be in a totally unfamiliar situation because he would be reuniting with his former head coach, John Harbaugh. Flacco's first year in the NFL came in 2008, which just happened to be Harbaugh's first year as head coach of the Ravens. The Harbaugh-Flacco combination had a lot of success during their 11 seasons together in Baltimore, including a Super Bowl win in 2012.
Yes, that was 14 years ago, and yes, Flacco is now 41, but the Giants don't need him to be their franchise quarterback. They need him to play at high level for 15 games and that's something he might be able to pull off. In six starts with the Bengals last season, Flacco averaged 272.7 passing yards per game while also throwing 13 touchdown passes compared to just four interceptions.
Flacco ending his career with the same head coach who was there at the beginning would also be kind of a poetic way for the former Super Bowl MVP to go out. Of course, for the Giants to get Flacco, the Bengals would have to be willing to trade him and there's no guarantee that would happen. Due to Joe Burrow's injury history, the Bengals would probably prefer to hold on to Flacco unless they got absolutely blown away by an offer.
That said, the two front offices are very familiar with each other thanks to the April trade that sent Dexter Lawrence to Cincinnati, so anything is possible.
Other quarterbacks who could be available for trade: J.J. McCarthy, Mac Jones. As I mentioned above, we stuck to two types of quarterbacks on our trade list: They either had to be mobile or familiar with the current coaching staff or both. If the Giants want classic pocket passer, it would probably just make sense to stick with Winston, who's in his second season with the team.
In terms of free agency, the Giants could give Jimmy Garoppolo a call, but at this point, he might not be a huge upgrade over Jameis Winston. There's also Russell Wilson, but he seems more than happy working with us here at CBS Sports.
The Giants do have a chance to save their season here. If they can find a QB who can play at a high level -- even if that QB ends up being Winston -- they could stay afloat all season. Over the next five weeks, the 1-1 Giants will play three games against teams that are currently 0-2 (Titans, Texans, and Commanders), along with a game against the Cardinals, so there are some winnable games that New York needs to take advantage of.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI’s Altman and Anthropic’s Amodei address UN security council
articles.title_zh: OpenAI’s Altman and Anthropic’s Amodei address UN security council
articles.content_orig:
Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic, heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies, addressed the United Nations security council on Wednesday in separate briefings on AI safety.
“We have a choice in front of us,” Altman told the council. “AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray.”
Altman and Amodei spoke as their companies face increasing scrutiny over the safety of their products. Public alarm over AI has grown in response to warnings from Anthropic researchers earlier this month that the technology could destroy humanity within the decade. Leaders of AI companies, including Altman and Amodei, have since called for a slowdown on advancing AI and more international cooperation on the technology’s safety standards.
Altman, who sat at the corner of the security council’s horseshoe-shaped table and spoke for about 10 minutes, touted AI’s benefits to productivity while also warning of its potential abuses. He advocated for governments to come together to build a future where AI is guided by democratic institutions, rather than one where people feel like the technology is “something being done to them”.
“If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone. They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said.
The OpenAI CEO’s speech contrasted with some of his company’s lobbying efforts and the political action committee of its president, Greg Brockman. The pro-AI Leading the Future PAC has accrued more than $100m and spent millions targeting candidates who support stronger regulation on the AI industry.
Altman’s speech also nodded to some of the concerns from Anthropic researchers about AI’s existential risk, warning the council against falling into “doomerism”. Altman argued there was instead a “middle path” through the safety debate that should be based on three principles: AI systems must remain under human control; AI must benefit people, from helping doctors treat patients to boosting entrepreneurs; and the technology must “empower people individually”.
Amodei, who addressed the council via video call, repeated many of the points that he made in a 12 September blog post that called for increased global cooperation and oversight of AI. He advocated for several forms of international agreements, including a ban on using AI to develop biological weapons and global standards for testing new AI models.
While Altman steered his address away from engaging with the warnings of existential risk that have made headlines this month, Amodei reiterated his concerns about developers losing control of AI while also framing his company as an industry leader on safety.
“If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Amodei said. “At Anthropic, we believe we have the best track record in the industry for preventing these risks”.
AI regulation has shot up the political agenda after researchers at OpenAI’s arch-rival Anthropic warned the technology could wipe out humanity within years. These concerns are a regular refrain within sections of the AI community, who fear the technology could trigger devastation for a variety of reasons ranging from aiding development of bioweapons to triggering a financial catastrophe. Earlier, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI, Google and Elon Musk.
Both Amodei and Altman have long cast themselves as stewards of AI and sought to shape how the technology is publicly received. Their companies are also jockeying for the lead in the AI race, with both eyeing potentially record-setting initial public offerings that would value each at more than $1.5tn.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft refreshes its smaller Surface Pro and Laptop with Qualcomm’s X2 Plus
articles.title_zh: Microsoft refreshes its smaller Surface Pro and Laptop with Qualcomm’s X2 Plus
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft is refreshing its Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface Laptop 13-inch devices with Qualcomm’s latest Snapdragon X2 Plus chips. The smaller Surface devices retain the same design and hardware features from last year, with faster and more capable chips inside and higher price tags (thanks RAMageddon!).
Microsoft refreshes its smaller Surface Pro and Laptop with Qualcomm’s X2 Plus
The Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface Laptop 13-inch both have better battery life and performance, but higher price tags.
While the 12-inch Surface Pro started at $799.99 last year, it’s debuting on October 13th at a starting price of $1,149.99. Likewise, the 13-inch Surface Laptop was originally priced at $899.99, but it’s up to $1,199.99 this time around. There’s no base 8GB model this time, causing some of the price increase, as both devices launch with a minimum of 16GB of RAM and can be configured up to 24GB.
Pricing aside, Microsoft is promising that the six-core Snapdragon X2 Plus chips will deliver up to 18 percent more efficient battery performance, more than 60 percent faster graphics performance, and up to 95 percent faster local AI inferencing on the built-in NPU.
That’s a lot of percentages, but what it equates to on these devices is better battery life and improved performance. On the Surface Pro 12-inch Second Edition, as Microsoft calls it, that means an extra hour of web browsing (up to 13 hours in total), and on the Surface Laptop 13-inch Second Edition it’s two extra hours of web browsing usage (up to 18 hours in total).
Microsoft is using similar displays on these models as last year, so the Surface Pro 12-inch has a 2196 x 1464 (220 PPI) LCD display that runs at up to 90Hz. The Surface Laptop 13-inch still ships with a 1920 x 1280 (178 PPI) display that only runs at 60Hz. Both displays have been upgraded from 400 nits of brightness to 500 nits, though.
Port selection remains the same, too. Both devices include two USB-C 3.2 ports, and the Surface Laptop 13-inch also has a USB-A 3.2 port and a 3.5mm headphone jack. Both also support Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4 connectivity.
I’m surprised that Microsoft hasn’t upgraded at least one of these smaller Surface devices with a haptic trackpad, particularly because Windows 11 now adds subtle haptic nudges, and the Surface Laptop Ultra ships with haptic feedback. Microsoft is launching a second edition of its Surface Mouse with integrated haptics, and you can read all about that here.
Microsoft is also bringing back the black color option for both of these smaller Surface devices, with platinum silver or violet colors available too. Both devices will also be sold to commercial customers, and the Surface Pro 12-inch will be available in an optional 5G configuration.

articles.title_orig: Former White Sox pitching coach Don Cooper, who led a World Series-winning rotation, dies at age 70
articles.title_zh: Former White Sox pitching coach Don Cooper, who led a World Series-winning rotation, dies at age 70
articles.content_orig:
Former longtime White Sox pitching coach Don Cooper has died at the age of 70, the team confirmed.
Cooper pitched for four major-league seasons, and began his second career as a Single-A pitching coach in the White Sox organization in 1988. But a midyear promotion to the major-league job in 2002 kicked off one of the most productive coaching runs in White Sox history.
“I will always believe him to be one of the best pitching coaches the game has seen,” former White Sox executive Ken Williams said via text. “The 2005 playoff pitching performances he coached are evidence, and epic, and will never be matched.”
Forever associated with the dominant starting rotation of the 2005 Sox team that captured the franchise’s first World Series title since 1917, Cooper remained the club’s pitching coach until he was fired alongside manager Rick Renteria after the 2020 season.
“Not news I wanted to wake up to today,” Paul Konerko said. “I can’t think about anything of my time with the White Sox without him being involved in it.”
Cooper’s tenure included Esteban Loaiza’s second-place finish in Cy Young voting in 2003, Chris Sale’s five straight All-Star appearances in a White Sox uniform, and the peak years of Mark Buehrle’s career, including his 2007 no-hitter and 2009 perfect game. When Buehrle, Jose Contreras, Jon Garland and Freddy Garcia closed out the 2005 American League Championship Series with four straight complete games, it was first time an MLB team had accomplished such a postseason feat since 1928, and none have managed it since.
“He fixed Jose Contreras,” A.J. Pierzynski told the Sun-Times. “He helped Mark Buehrle become a borderline, arguably a Hall-of-Famer. Jon Garland, he made better. Brandon McCarthy, helped have a long career. Freddy Garcia, he helped with stuff. Bobby Jenks, he fixed, Cliff Politte, Neal Cotts. The list goes on and on of people that he helped, not only on the field, but off the field.”
Especially as the work of pitching instruction changed over time, Sox pitchers reiterated that Cooper’s greatest strength lay in a building block of coaching: he instilled confidence in his players.
“The guys loved him,” Sox general manager Chris Getz said. “When pitchers reflect back on their careers, they really remember how he made them feel.”
At the height of his powers, as a collection of pitchers rose from obscurity to success like Jose Quintana’s emergence from minor-league free agency, Matt Thornton becoming an All-Star reliever, or Gavin Floyd going from a 7.00 ERA to a mid-rotation fixture, an enduring adage became popular among White Sox fans for every new pitching addition: “Coop’ll fix ’em.”
“He seemed to me, part of the fabric of the Chicago White Sox,” broadcaster Steve Stone said. “I don’t think we’ll ever see the likes of him again.”
Chicago Sun-TimesWhite Sox reporter

articles.title_orig: The Book Started as a Steamy Star Wars Fanfic. Now the Movie Adaptation Is Here. Uh-oh.
articles.title_zh: The Book Started as a Steamy Star Wars Fanfic. Now the Movie Adaptation Is Here. Uh-oh.
articles.content_orig:
In Sex Reviews, writers offer a sober critical assessment of the sex scenes in new films and television series. This installment contains spoilers for The Love Hypothesis.
While the covers of Ali Hazelwood’s bestselling novels blend right in with other contemporary millennial romance fare, what’s between the pages is distinctive for the genre. Hazelwood, a former neuroscience professor, favors a combination of STEM milieus (two books set at Stanford, others at NASA’s Johnson Space Center, MIT, and an Arctic research center) and STEM heroes and heroines (every person in a Hazelwood book is an engineer, a scientist, or a game developer) with what can sometimes be extremely detailed and extensive sex scenes. Her Not in Love series and her campus romance Deep End can barely be read in public, so flushed will your face become. The Hazelwood fantasy is something that can only be described as “best-case Bay Area”: nerds with broad chests who, when tested, display an unexpected ability to apply themselves … both in and out of bed.
Now, the Amazon Prime romance adaptation machine has come for Hazelwood. The Love Hypothesis, her debut novel from 2021, is about Olive, an up-till-now-sorta-asexual biology Ph.D. candidate at Stanford, who ends up “fake dating” a tenured professor, Adam, a cranky stickler who’s every student’s bête noire. (Olive needs to convince a friend she’s partnered so the friend will feel OK dating Olive’s former crush; Adam needs to prove to his department he’s committed to the university, not a flight risk, so that they will release his research funds.) Adam is not on Olive’s dissertation committee, the book hastens to stipulate, meaning this relationship does not constitute a violation of academic integrity—though in the course of the plot, their alliance raises several ethical questions. (Hazelwood, among other predilections—a Hazelwood heroine tends to be physically tiny; a hero is always huge—loves an age gap.) Prime’s highly anticipated movie version of The Love Hypothesis stars Lili Reinhart (best known as Betty from Riverdale) and British actor Tom Bateman as these fake-then-real lovers. But does the movie—could any movie—give us that good old Hazelwood buzz? Slate senior writer Rebecca Onion and Slate staff writer Nadira Goffe discuss.
1:18:13 Olive and Adam Finally Do It
Nadira Goffe: Well, what can I say, Rebecca? We’re 90 minutes into this 112-minute film, and we’re only just now getting our first sex scene. But this isn’t just the first sex scene, it’s also the only one in the whole movie. Normally, I would be OK with that, but come on, this is an adaptation of an Ali Hazelwood book! Let’s do better at understanding our source material here. It doesn’t help that this moment also feels like the only true instance of physical intimacy the couple displays throughout the film’s nearly two-hour run time. As is expected with any fake-dating plot, the earlier parts of the movie are riddled with moments of forced intimacy, where Adam and Olive struggle to put on a show for their friends and colleagues before they’re comfortable with each other: Olive awkwardly puts sunscreen on a shirtless Adam’s back, Adam hesitantly kisses Olive’s forehead, etc.
Admittedly, the few kisses they share before this are good. But that’s about all The Love Hypothesis has to offer us outside of this intimate scene right here. There is no moment of: We started off with a normal kiss but got carried away. At no point do the protagonists struggle not to touch each other as their chemistry evolves, something that any good romance should deliver. Before they get biblical here, they don’t even hold hands unless someone else is looking.
In fact, there’s not much lead-up at all, until Olive and Adam are getting dinner after presenting at a science conference in Boston. They hold hands, but pull away when they realize it, and go on pretending they were never touching. On the way home, when Olive’s high heels begin killing her feet, Adam carries her, bridal style, all the way back to the hotel where, due to some usual romance-plot kerfuffles, the two have been forced to share a room. Olive, who forgot to pack pajamas, changes into a big T-shirt that shows most of her legs; Adam, who sits on the edge of his bed, gets caught off guard by his sexual attraction and suggests they just go to bed. Olive, though, steps in between his legs and kisses him. Rebecca, you’ve read the book much more recently than I have. What do you think about what happens next?
Rebecca Onion: Nadira, I am somewhat ashamed to reveal that, much like Olive and Adam, we have faked everyone out—in this case, our beloved Sex Reviews readers, who expect to read our highbrow analysis of more than just one mid sex scene. But we did it to make a point about the kinds of romance novels that make good adaptations for a romance-hungry streamer like Prime. Sure, in The Love Hypothesis (novel version), the percentage of pages devoted to sex are relatively few for a Hazelwood—it’s no Deep End (seriously, that one’s for the truly thirsty). But if you look back at the major sex scene in the novel, with my apologies to any gentle readers of Slate.com who don’t think we mean it when we say Sex Reviews, you find moments like these:
- Adam “fits her entire breast in his mouth. All of it.”
- During the lead-up to their interlude, Adam “cups his cock almost absentmindedly, stroking and gripping every once in a while.”
- Adam slides Olive’s underwear to the side and finds she’s aroused: “She was glistening, swollen and plump to her own eyes, way too far ahead, considering that they’d barely done anything.” (This idea, that a woman could be so wet it’s embarrassing, is a classic romance novel trope.)
- They have trouble fitting his penis, which is “enormous” like every romance-novel penis, into her vagina. They figure it out when Adam “angles Olive’s knee just so, spreading her legs in a way she simply hadn’t thought of.” (This is the Ali Hazelwood “competent people are competent at everything” STEM kink in action.)
- Adam goes down on Olive and “sucks on one of her lips with a loud, wet noise” and then inserts his tongue … needless to say, she loves it.
OK. I will stop. I know we are not Sex Reviewing the Ali Hazelwood novel The Love Hypothesis. But I need the contrast between this sex scene and what you get in the Prime movie to be clear. Because what you get in the Prime movie is a whispery pop song, a bunch of kissing, two hot people sort of softly lit on hotel sheets, then like 10 seconds of cunnilingus, some missionary, and some girl-on-top action, all resulting in a vaguely pleased look on Lili Reinhart’s face. The entire fevered, super-juicy vibe of the many pages of sex in the novel is completely gone.
The other major thing that’s different is that, in the book, Olive is almost asexual, rarely attracted to anyone, so having sex with someone is a big deal, and she and Adam talk about this fact a lot more before they do all that work to fit his enormous penis in there. All of that “I’m telling my new lover my deepest secrets” sweaty, intimate stuff is pretty much gone in this movie.
I just am not really sure, now that I’ve seen the proof, that Hazelwood romance novels are a good match for Amazon Prime. I feel like they wanted a regular rom-com, and they made The Love Hypothesis into one! Am I overthinking this, Nadira?
Nadira: You know that meme from the 2005 film version of Narnia where the lion, Aslan, tells the White Witch, “Do not cite the Deep Magic to me, Witch, I was there when it was written”? Well, this is one of those moments where the deep magic did need to be cited, and there’s no one better at consulting our primary sources and getting textual than you, Rebecca! Thank you for this service.
To your question: I think risking scandalizing our readers with your astute rundown of the novel scene was needed precisely because you’re not overthinking this at all! A great deal of Hazelwood’s work subsists—na

articles.title_orig: McDonald's bets on hand-breaded chicken, AI drive-throughs to fend off Burger King
articles.title_zh: McDonald's bets on hand-breaded chicken, AI drive-throughs to fend off Burger King
articles.content_orig:
CHICAGO, IL — McDonald's (MCD) is making a long-term bet on artificial intelligence, hand-breaded chicken, and a return of 90s-style restaurants to regain customers who left for other chains, like Burger King.
At its investor day in Chicago, the fast food giant unveiled a new set of ambitious goals and investments as part of its growth plan, following a rocky second quarter that resulted in 0.8% US same-store sales growth versus Burger King's whopping 8.5% growth.
McDonald's said it plans to invest $8.5 billion through 2036 tosupport restaurant tech updates with rent relief and capital. It intends to deliver roughly $5 billion of that investment by 2030.
"You start with the opportunity, which we think is really clear and compelling," McDonald's CFO Ian Borden told Yahoo Finance. "We think it's going to provide a really strong return for our operators and for McDonald's."
Franchisees are encouraged to adopt the plan in phases. One franchisee operator told Yahoo Finance they are skating on thin margins with higher ingredient, labor, and rent costs, making another costly redesign difficult, especially in a high-interest-rate environment.
"Certainly, it's a different interest rate environment with franchisees," McDonald's CEO Chris Kempczinski told Yahoo Finance. "Back 10 years ago, … it was practically like free money."
However, he added, "the benefit is franchisees, even though they're taking on the money, they've got … that sort of halo of McDonald's. … The interest rate that they're getting charged by banks or will get charged by banks is going to be significantly less than if they were Joe's Burger joint."
Operators are expected to update the restaurants' look and feel as part of a remodel cycle every 10 years, per McDonald's, and Kempczinski said those costs typically add up to $400,000 to $450,000 per restaurant.
Deploying the suite of McDonald's productivity improvements will cost franchise operators an additional $800,000 per US restaurant. For international markets, it will run around $650,000 to $750,000.
"It's about just keeping the restaurant looking up to date … paint the walls, fix the roof, make sure the parking lots are in good shape, all of that is part of that investment," Kempczinski said. "The remainder of the investment, the roughly [$800,000] … or so, is all tied to sales driving or productivity driving initiatives."
It remains to be seen whether the strategic growth plan can turn around McDonald's stock.McDonald's shares have struggled to entice investors to take a bite this year, declining 18% year to date, compared to a 4.6% gain for Burger King's parent company stock, Restaurant Brands International (QSR), and 13% gain for the S&P 500 (^GSPC).
McDonald's stock fell 5% on Wednesday.
Chicken, but 'Make it Golden'
Part of the strategy is a commitment called "Make it Golden," which doubles down on food, hospitality, and employee training.
After Burger King overhauled its chicken nugget recipe, McDonald's is doing something similar by piloting hand-breaded chicken.
The chicken comes frozen, marinated, dipped in batter, and hand-breaded, Jacques Mignault, McDonald's Global Chief Restaurant Officer, told Yahoo Finance. The secret is to flip the chicken seven times.
McDonald's is targeting a 1.5% gain in market share, with the chicken and beverage categories leading the way (crafted sodas are another major focus for McDonald's). It expects to add more US restaurants to the hand-breaded chicken pilot in early 2027.
Mignault said the new chicken is "actually beating the competition from a taste and quality standpoint" in Asian markets. He added that the company has also started testing bone-in wings.
McDonalds also aims to maintain its beef market share leadership after leaning into the Big Arch Burger, which went viral earlier this year after a video of CEO Chris Kempczinski tasting the burger prompted other fast food CEOs to respond.
McDonald's PlayPlace makes a comeback
Gone is the modernized, gray box design McDonald's implemented years ago.
Now, McDonald's is reintroducing a smaller PlayPlace, featuring a slide, jungle gym, and analog toys (no, there's no ball pit).
The goal is for families to visit restaurants more often and spend more when they do. Foot traffic at McDonald's has faltered. During the week of Sept. 7, McDonald's foot traffic fell 3.1% year over year, compared to a 2.8% decline in overall quick-service restaurants and a 7.1% gain for Burger King, per Placer.ai.
"Our customers were telling us, look, McDonald's used to be fun, just inject some of the personality back into the look and feel of restaurants," Jill McDonald, executive vice president and global chief restaurant experience officer, told Yahoo Finance.
The back of the house is also getting an upgrade with AI technology, dubbed ArchIQ.
Think kitchens and drive-throughs integrated with artificial intelligence, powered by Google Edge (GOOG). Even artificial intelligence will be used to ensure the McFlurry Machine does not go down.
CFO Borden said this is different than the company's previous partnership with IBM (IBM), which ended in 2024.
"A few years ago, it was a different technology platform," Borden said. "That large language model that we are building with Google just allows the learning to get sharper and sharper. … We are already far advanced versus where we were several years ago with what we were doing previously."
The use of AI technology is a game changer, executives say, and will contribute to a part of a 250 basis point improvement in gross restaurant-level efficiency gains, which the company said is equivalent to roughly $100,000 in annual cash flow for the average US restaurant.
The drive-through technology is expected to save restaurants' 50-plus labor hours per week, McDonald's said.
Brooke DiPalma is a reporter for Yahoo Finance. Follow her on X at @BrookeDiPalma or email her at bdipalma@yahoofinance.com.

articles.title_orig: Venezuelan man shot by ICE officer needs surgery to remove the bullet, U.S. Rep. Greg Casar says
articles.title_zh: Venezuelan man shot by ICE officer needs surgery to remove the bullet, U.S. Rep. Greg Casar says
articles.content_orig:
Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, who was shot Sunday by federal immigration officers in Austin, needs surgery to remove the bullet lodged near his spine, U.S. Rep. Greg Casar said Wednesday after visiting the Venezuelan man in a detention center in Pearsall.
Casar said in a news conference that Garces Perez saw a specialist Wednesday who recommended surgery. He also received his first injection of pain medication one hour before the visit, said Casar, D-Austin.
Casar said Garces Perez, who was in high spirits, was in a wheelchair with his left arm in a sling and had heavy bruising on his torso and debilitating pain on his left side. Medical staff at the ICE detention facility had been cleaning Garces Perez’s wound two to three times per day, Casar said.
“This person needs a doctor, not a deportation or a detention center,” he said.
Also Wednesday, news reports said the federal immigration officer who shot Garces Perez was not using a body camera during the Sunday incident.
The recent U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement recruit — who has not been publicly identified — was issued a body camera but was not wearing it when he fired at Garces Perez, according to The Atlantic, The Washington Post and NBC News, which quoted unnamed current and former officials with the Department of Homeland Security.
It’s not clear why the ICE officer was not using the device during the shooting, which left the 28-year-old man with a bullet lodged to his back. Homeland Security didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Another ICE officer involved in Garces Perez’s arrest did use his body camera, but its footage didn’t capture the shooting, according to NBC News.
“You need to answer why your agents are not turning their body cams on,” Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, the injured man’s attorney, told DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin in a Tuesday post on X. “Release the footage immediately!”
The reports came amid heightened focus on the availability of such devices for ICE officers, following the lack of body-cam footage in the recent fatal shootings of immigrants like that of 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo on July 7.
In that Houston case, acting ICE Director David Venturella said the officers involved in the shooting didn’t have body-worn cameras or dashboard cameras. DHS said in a July 12 statement that body cameras had been sent to more than half of the field offices and the rest would receive them in the next 60 days.
Earlier this month, Mullin said the agency was “on track by the end of September” to equip all officers who are in the field with a body camera.
“It’s for our safety and the public safety, too,” he added at a news conference.
ICE policy also gives the agency critical control over what to release in cases of severe or fatal use of force, saying that such footage would only be made public if “it is in the best interests of the agency.”
On Sunday, Garces Perez was working as a DoorDash delivery driver when he was shot by an ICE officer during a traffic stop in North Austin, which included a brief vehicle pursuit.
Lincoln-Goldfinch said he entered the U.S. legally in 2024 via the CBP One app and applied for asylum. But the man missed his immigration court hearing after the notice was sent to the wrong address, leading to a final order of removal. The attorney added that his work permit expired in December.
A day after the shooting, Garces Perez said an unmarked SUV sideswiped him twice before he realized that ICE officers were trying to pull him over. He said he did a U-turn under a freeway underpass when the SUV struck his blue Toyota Camry. That’s when the SUVs turned on their lights and sirens, he added.
Garces Perez said he then asked the officers if he could stop somewhere safer. He said an officer told him no, then he felt one shot to his back.
On Tuesday, DHS said the shooting followed a “dangerous attempt to evade arrest.”
“Resisting officers and evading arrest is dangerous for our officers, illegal aliens, and the public,” the department’s statement said. “We remind the public that resisting officers and evading arrest is a felony and a federal crime.”
Meanwhile, Garces Perez’s attorneys have filed a petition to block his deportation and get him out of ICE detention. A federal judge set a hearing in San Antonio on Sept. 30 for the case and ordered Garces Perez to make an appearance.

articles.title_orig: Tigrayan Forces Mobilize Against the Central Government in Ethiopia
articles.title_zh: Tigrayan Forces Mobilize Against the Central Government in Ethiopia
articles.content_orig:
Ethiopia and Tigray accuse each of launching offensives, fuelling fears of new war
Ethiopia's government and the party in control of the northern region of Tigray have accused each other of launching offensives, escalating fears of a return to full-scale conflict.
Getachew Reda, a cabinet minister and adviser to Ethiopia's prime minister, said Tigrayan fighters had taken control of federally administered airports in Tigray and launched offensives in neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions.
Earlier, the Tigrayan authorities said their forces had been forced to enter a "defensive war". The statement followed reports of drone strikes in Tigray.
The two-year war in Tigray ended in 2022 - but over recent months both sides have been accusing each other of violating a peace deal.
It was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the African Union's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine.
On Sunday, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray, announced an alliance with six other armed groups in Ethiopia to remove the government in Addis Ababa.
"It is rather heartbreaking to learn that, despite efforts by many, including the international community, to avoid yet another round of war in Tigray, the TPLF leadership early this morning launched an all-out offensive against government positions in Afar and Amhara," Getachew said in a statement shared on social media.
The adviser to Prime Minster Abiy Ahmed previously led Tigray's interim administration, but he fell out with the TPLF in 2025 and joined the federal government.
Following the seizure of the airports, Ethiopian Airlines has cancelled all flights to Tigray.
Residents of Tigray's main city of Mekelle told the BBC that local forces had taken over control of the city's airport from the national police early on Wednesday.
This followed reports of drone strikes in Tigray in recent days.
The chairperson of the Africa Union Commission, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, has called for an "immediate de-escalation" and for both sides to resume talks.
The US ambassador to Ethiopia condemned the TPLF for making "the poor decision to launch a large-scale offensive", describing it as an "unwinnable fight".
On Tuesday, a strike in the southern town of Alamata killed at least 14 people and injured 22 others, according to the Tigrayan authorities.
The town's mayor, Mogos Shiferaw, told the BBC that more than five drones and one fighter jet had carried out more than 21 strikes starting at around 03:30.
"This caused a lot of psychological trauma in our city and our people were in a state of panic," he said.
Mogos said all those killed and injured were civilians, accusing federal forces of targeting two secondary schools.
He believed they were struck on suspicion that they were being used by Tigrayan forces.
But the mayor said the schools, which had served as federal military bases during the civil war, were unoccupied as the academic year had not yet begun.
The BBC has not independently verified the allegations and the government has not commented on the alleged strikes.
On Wednesday, the Tigray authorities accused Addis Ababa of launching an "open invasion" of the region, urging people to support the regional forces and maintain unity.
It further accused the government of violating international humanitarian and human rights laws, saying public services and critical infrastructure had been disrupted.
Meanwhile, the US State Department's Bureau of African Affairs has condemned a separate drone strike that it said took place on Monday, targeting a convoy of Catholic vehicles carrying food aid.
It called for an investigation and urged all parties to resolve their differences through dialogue and take steps to prevent similar incidents.
Both Addis Ababa and TPLF leaders have faced criticism over delays in implementing key provisions of the Pretoria Agreement, the AU-brokered deal that formally ended the conflict in November 2022.
In July, Prime Minister Abiy accused the TPLF of preparing for renewed conflict during an address to parliament.
Just before the general election in May, which was not held in Tigray because of the security situation, the TPLF restored its pre-war administration, disbanding an interim one appointed by Abiy.
There have also been reports that the TPLF has been forcibly recruiting young men to join its forces.

articles.title_orig: ChatGPT mobile app gets voice-based agentic features
articles.title_zh: ChatGPT mobile app gets voice-based agentic features
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI announced on Wednesday that it is bringing voice-based agentic features to mobile, allowing users to trigger workflows like drafting documents or summarizing emails.
Plus and Pro users will be able to use the Work tab on their phone to create a document, draft an email, or summarize Slack messages, for instance. These subscribers can do things like build sites, create presentations, use the cloud browser, and also access other areas like finances in ChatGPT. Free and Go users, meanwhile, will get to work with plugins and connected apps.
OpenAI said ChatGPT’s voice conversations will have richer text output. Plus, users will be able to switch between text and voice easily. They can also start working on a conversation on the go and resume it on desktop.
The feature arrives as an increasing number of users are turning to voice to issue commands to AI assistants for complex tasks.
In July, OpenAI launched its new conversational model GPT-Live, and later the company integrated it with the desktop app to let users use their voice to complete tasks in the Work tab or build apps in the Codex tab. The new rollout brings similar capabilities to the mobile app.
Recently, Anthropic made the handoff between mobile and desktop easier and also merged its Cowork and Chat interface. But OpenAI is still keeping chat and workspaces separate.

articles.title_orig: China's 80% Grip on Iranian Oil Looms Over Trump-Xi Summit
articles.title_zh: China's 80% Grip on Iranian Oil Looms Over Trump-Xi Summit
articles.content_orig:
Ahead of a high-stakes US-China summit planned for September 24 at the White House, Beijing appears to be spotlighting its influence over Iran to gain leverage during negotiations with its chief geopolitical rival.
Expectations for a US-China breakthrough on Iran at the upcoming summit in Washington are low. Trump has signaled a focus on economic outcomes for this meeting with Xi and the Chinese leader has reciprocated by assembling a delegation of top business executives.
But in the run-up to the meeting, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghch in Beijing on September 16. The meeting was the fourth time the two men have spoken in the past three months.
During their meeting, Wang noted that Beijing and Tehran are “comprehensive strategic partners,” an asymmetric relationship that favors Beijing.
China is Iran's largest trading partner and the destination for over 80 percent of its seaborne oil exports, according to commodities analytics firm Kpler. Yet Iran accounts for just 1 percent of China’s overall global trade, per Chinese government data.
China, Wang said, “is also willing to strengthen dialogue and cooperation with Iran and safeguard Iran's legitimate rights and interests.”
The Chinese foreign minister urged “all parties” to take measures to swiftly “reopen” the Strait of Hormuz -- a waterway that before the US-Iran war was the route for about one-fifth of the global oil and gas supply -- but stopped short of directly pressuring Iran.
Nor did he offer a concrete mediation plan.
“China isn’t going to do the heavy lifting” to bring the US and Iran to the table again, Elizabeth Freund Larus, an adjunct senior fellow at the Pacific Forum think tank, told RFE/RL.
She noted that China benefits geopolitically from the conflict’s toll on US military resources even though Beijing faces economic pressure from higher energy and raw material costs.
The Iran war has cost the Pentagon more than $38 billion through August 1, according to the Congressional Budget Office.
Further, in recent months, Washington has diverted significant military assets from the Indo-Pacific region to the Middle East. The United States now lacks a deployed aircraft carrier in the Western Pacific for the first time since World War II, unnerving American allies wary of China’s massive military buildup.
At the same time, Beijing faces surging oil prices. Shanghai crude oil futures hit a record 929.4 yuan ($137.80) per barrel this month after Iranian-backed proxies launched drone attacks that damaged Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline.
To a certain extent, China’s strategic stockpiling of oil helps insulate it from price increases.
The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) estimates that Beijing injected an average of 1.1 million barrels a day into its national oil storage last year, which gave it a total of 1.4 million barrels as of December 2025. That’s three times the size of America’s Strategic Petroleum Reserve.
Still, the buffer provided by the reserve only goes so far.
Bill Bishop, a Washington-based China expert and commentator, noted in the September 16 edition of his Sinocism newsletter that the “global economic impact of another huge petrochemical price surge would damage the export markets the PRC economy needs.”
“China for sure wants the war to end -- a higher oil price is in no one’s interest, but the question is who should bear the cost to bring it to an end?” Yun Sun, director of the Stimson Center’s China Program in Washington, said in an interview.
“If China is to press Iran, it will beg the question as for what the US and Iran will do to de-escalate and stabilize, and meet Iran’s need for security. So far, the content on that is pretty thin.”
While China is officially neutral in the Iran war, it has provided significant support to Tehran.
Crucially, Beijing’s purchase of Tehran’s oil in large quantities has extended an economic lifeline to the beleaguered Iranian regime. To circumvent punishing US sanctions, China uses a covert, barter-like trade mechanism, according to Reuters. Since transactions do not travel through the Western-dominated global financial system, they evade US oversight.
The administration of US President Donald Trump has repeatedly pressed China to cooperate with sanctions on Iran. After the administration intensified those sanctions in late August, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that those who “enable” Tehran should not “discount the cost of testing Washington.”
The US has several options to compel better Chinese cooperation on Iran sanctions.
The first is blacklisting independent Chinese oil refineries that have purchased Iranian oil in large quantities. Thus far, it has sanctioned five such firms. Washington has also sanctioned dozens of China-linked shipping firms and vessels for maritime trade with Iran.
These measures have caused substantial commercial obstacles and compliance pressure.
However, Iran and its Chinese buyers can evade the sanctions. Tehran uses a so-called “shadow fleet” of old oil tankers and shell companies that covertly exports petroleum. Beijing has also ordered its companies not to comply with the US sanctions.
Washington, however, has a more substantial economic weapon in its arsenal: its dominance of the global financial system. The Trump administration could ban sanction-busting Chinese state banks from using the dollar. That move would have a devastating effect on China’s economy.
Yet given the substantial US-China economic relationship, “the broad imposition of sanctions on China’s financial institutions could be very disruptive to the US economy too,” Taipei-based lawyer and political risk consultant Ross Darrell Feingold said in an interview.
At the same time, US financial firms operating in China would likely be subject to severe Chinese retaliation.
In the event the Trump administration is seriously considering sanctions on large Chinese banks, “these financial institutions will make their concerns known to the White House,” he says.
Part of Beijing’s rationale for defying sanctions rests on its interpretation of international law. “There is no UN sanction against normal trade between China and Iran,” the Stimson Center’s Sun says, adding, “And China does not accept the legality of US unilateral sanctions.”
For Washington, one of the most concerning aspects of China’s pro-Iran stance is that it extends to the military domain.
“China plays a critical but often overlooked role in sustaining Iran's defense industrial base,” US-China Economic and Security Review Commission Vice Chair Mike Kuiken said in a July statement. That role includes providing components for Iranian Shahed drones and ballistic missiles as well as sodium perchlorate, a chemical needed for rocket fuel. Tehran uses China's BeiDou satellite navigation system to direct military operations.
Beijing denies supporting Iran militarily or providing it with intelligence.
China’s approach to supplying dual-use equipment (which has both commercial and military applications) to Iran as well as Iranian access to Chinese satellite navigation technology “is shaped by a tension between Beijing's interest in supporting Iranian capabilities in key areas and its desire to minimize potential blowback,” John Van Oudenaren, a research analyst for the technology consultancy BluePath Labs in Washington, told RFE/RL.
China is wary of risking additional major US sanctions on Chinese entities or a deterioration in relations with Washington and its allies, he added.
In recent weeks, Trump has downplayed Beijing’s close ties with Tehran, telling reporters at the White House on September 4 that “they’re [China] not really involved” in the Iran war. Trump has previously said Xi promised him that China wouldn’t provide Iran with military equipment.
"Maybe they [Trump and Xi] will have a quiet discussion about the value of sanctions” when they meet, Carice Witte, an Israel-based China expert and executive director at the SIGN

articles.title_orig: Meta's Muse reignites AI disruption fears. Traders are targeting this brokerage stock as next casualty
articles.title_zh: Meta's Muse reignites AI disruption fears. Traders are targeting this brokerage stock as next casualty
articles.content_orig:
Meta's latest consumer AI product is sending such big shockwaves through the market that it's even inflaming a long-time rivalry in the brokerage business between 55-year old investing giant Charles Schwab, and Robinhood, an icon of the post-Covid trading boom among young investors.
Shares of Schwab fell 6% Tuesday, touching the lowest since early July and the stock is now down more than 8% since Meta announced Muse. Meanwhile, Robinhood's stock was higher, notching anotheryear-to-date high. In May, the company launched AI agents that can now trade and manage portfolios on behalf of users.
Shares of sprawling wealth management business LPL Financial Holdings dropped 7% Tuesday, financial services firm Raymond James Financial shed 3.5 percent, and Interactive Brokers slipped 1% as the State Street Financial Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLF) lost 2% and is now down 6 percent from highs made earlier this month. Higher interest rates may not be helping.
It's not the first time an AI product has jostled the group – in February, the same group of stocks dropped when tech platform Altruist said its platform `Hazel' can create tax-planning strategies for individuals and advisors. Schwab stock recovered some in the months after – LPL has not.
"Schwab's an interesting animal," said Jimmy Lee, founder and CEO of The Wealth Consulting Group, a Las Vegas-based advisor that oversees $8 billion in assets. "To us in the advisor space they're kind of neutral and figuring out how best to protect their market share. I don't think Meta brings a lot of competition from the custodian perspective because it's not like Altruist's platform, but there is a lot of disruption that's going to happen among financial middle-men that charge fees for billing, reporting, trading, etc."
Meta's AI assistant says it won't trade for users or give financial advice, but when queried with how it might mimic the work of a financial advisor or broker, lists abilities including tracking investments and progress towards goals, as well as analyzing how portfolio holdings fit together.
Last week, Schwab Advisor Services, the company's platform for registered investment advisors, announced it is working with Anthropic to create Claude for Financial Advisors. In May, the company launched an AI tool that includes tailored analysis from the company's research arm. Representatives from Schwab did not respond to a request for comment. Robinhood reps declined to add to this story.
Robinhood's bounce on Tuesday brings its stock to a 10% rally on the year after dropping more than 40% in the first three months. The retail-focused brokerage, which also offers digital banking and advisory services, is up 1200 percent the past three years. Schwab stock is up 83 percent and the XLF is up 65 percent.
"AI and tokenization threaten to dismantle the frictions that legacy financial intermediaries have historically monetized," Piper Sandler analyst Patrick Moley wrote in a note in April. "Schwab's reliance on low-yielding sweep cash puts it squarely in the crosshairs."
Bets increase against Schwab
Judging by options-market flows around the stocks on Tuesday, the threat to Schwab may be a lasting one.
Options volume in Schwab was more than five times the average, with nearly twice as many puts bought vs. calls, Cboe LiveVol data show. The most popular contract to buy was the 90-strike put expiring mid-January, a bet the stock drops another 13% the next three months. To be sure, there was one big counter-trade sale of the Oct. 16 95-strike puts.
What's arguably most notable is in Robinhood options, sentiment was the opposite – traders bought twice as many calls as puts with more than 80 percent of the $95 million in premium traded tied to calls. The most heavily traded contract was the 125-strike call expiring on Friday.
"Gen Z and millennials gravitate towards platforms like Robinhood and Public which is why those platforms ship products so quickly," Gav Blaxberg, founder of Wolf Financial, a popular online trader enclave, said in a call. "Robinhood has built enough trust rebuilding its brand since GameStop and they're allowing agents to trade literally everything."
Correction: The founder of Wolf Financial is Gav Blaxberg. An earlier version of this story misspelled his name.

articles.title_orig: Without Caleb Williams, Bears enter Week 3 aggravated after sloppy Sunday
articles.title_zh: Without Caleb Williams, Bears enter Week 3 aggravated after sloppy Sunday
articles.content_orig:
It was the scream heard round the NFL. As well as in a whole lot of Chicago living rooms.
The Bears’ Caleb Williams collapsed in a heap without being contacted on a drenched Soldier Field as his team was driving for a potentially game-winning touchdown Sunday. As he fell, he let out a yowl. Fans feared the worst after he was carted off the field, naturally, and social-media speculation abounded. Amateur diagnosticians concluded everything from a torn Achilles tendon to a torn ACL to a torn hamstring.
So when the great news arrived the following day that Williams had “merely” strained his hamstring and was likely to only miss maybe a couple of games, the phony-outrage and ridicule machine revved up fast on social media.
Amid memes galore, the gist of the online criticism was that Williams was somehow soft for reacting so dramatically in the moment to his injury when it turned out not to be season-ending or something. Naturally, that prompted huffy defenses of Williams from those in Chicago’s sports talk galaxy.
Two days later, the “debate” was still raging.
We’re all for dopey sports beefs waged in good fun as a distraction from the negativity that permeates so much of our national discourse these days.
But judging an athlete’s pain response at the moment of their injury? Inappropriate to say the least.
No one criticizing Williams from the outside knows what he was experiencing nor do they know whether his reaction wasn’t in part frustration at not being able to finish a game which he was on the cusp of winning, despite the Bears’ sorry play throughout much of the day.
And anyone who has watched him play knows that questioning his toughness is absurd. As a rookie, he was sacked 68 times! A dubious Bears franchise record for sure, but he got up each time and played every game that season.
Meanwhile, Jaxson Dart, the New York Giants’ quarterback, limped off the field Monday night with barely a grimace after a crunching hit by two Los Angeles Rams. Word Tuesday afternoon was that he might need surgery. We assume the social-media pain specialists will waste little time with their toughness assessments of the two young quarterbacks by comparing the two contrasting outcomes with their in-the-moment reactions.
These are the kinds of yammerings that in pre-internet times would have occurred in a barroom or a living room, leaving the utterer to embarrass himself only in the company of those around him. Now, once posted, these insta-reactions and hot takes are there for all the online world to see.
These are extraordinary athletes who put their bodies and even their future health on the line for our entertainment. Bottom line is that most regular human beings absorbing the sort of punishment Williams and other pro football players experience on the regular would find themselves in traction.

articles.title_orig: China's Xi kicks off state visit to Washington with a rare planeside welcome from Trump
articles.title_zh: China's Xi kicks off state visit to Washington with a rare planeside welcome from Trump
articles.content_orig: By — Michelle L. Price, Associated Press Michelle L. Price, Associated Press By — Didi Tang, Associated Press Didi Tang, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/chinas-xi-kicks-off-state-visit-to-washington-with-a-rare-planeside-welcome-from-trump Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter China's Xi kicks off state visit to Washington with a rare planeside welcome from Trump World Updated on Sep 23, 2026 8:51 PM EDT — Published on Sep 23, 2026 11:16 AM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington on Wednesday, where he was met with a rare planeside greeting from President Donald Trump after their top officials agreed to extend a trade truce until January. READ MORE: Why Trump is rolling out the red carpet for Xi after years of slamming China Trump's Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the extension of the truce — under which the countries agreed to scale back tariffs and refrain from imposing new trade restrictions — during a Fox News Channel interview as Trump welcomed Xi at Joint Base Andrews just outside Washington. "I don't know whether a bigger deal can be done. I don't know whether we will just roll the current deal," Bessent said in the interview, noting the extension to Jan. 10 could give the leaders more time to talk about the issues at upcoming international summits in China in November and Florida in December. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Trade has been one of the biggest flashpoints between the two superpowers, along with artificial intelligence, Trump's war with Iran and China's designs on Taiwan. But much of Xi's three-day visit is expected to be far more about pomp than substance, starting with Trump's decision to greet Xi as he landed, rather than waiting for him to drive up to the White House. READ MORE: As China and U.S. compete for AI dominance, both have shared concerns over safety A 100-foot (30 meter) long red carpet was unfurled at the bottom of the staircase placed at the door of Xi's plane. A 21-person honor guard was arrayed on the sides of the carpet and Trump and first lady Melania Trump stood near a staircase on the side of the plane, where they greeted Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, with handshakes. The welcome ceremony also included a flyover by two B-1 bombers, platoons from each military service, and a presentation of the flags and anthems of both countries. Trump and his wife spoke to their counterparts, but their words could not be heard. Trump, who wore gloves and an overcoat though it was a relatively warm 63 degrees Fahrenheit (17 degrees Celsius) outside, removed one of his gloves to shake hands with Xi. At one point, he slapped Xi on the back and said something to him that was inaudible. "I think they appreciate it, tremendous people," Trump told reporters after he returned to the White House Wednesday evening. In a statement marking his arrival in the U.S., China's leader wrote that his country and the U.S. "should be partners, not rivals. Achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand and the two countries can contribute to each other's success, thereby benefiting the wider world." Some Republicans have questioned the optics of the visit Beyond using the visit to try to keep "strategic stability" between the two countries, Trump has lavished praise on Xi as a "great leader" and described a warm relationship with the man he has called a friend. That is all while he has given Xi a pass on many issues. Sen. Roger Wicker, chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, criticized the "lavish welcome." Wicker, R-Miss., said during a speech Tuesday in the Senate that Trump should not have invited the Chinese leader "based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party." Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the U.S. and China must interact at the highest levels because the countries are "the two largest economies in the world" and "probably the two most powerful militaries in the world." Danny Russel, a former U.S. diplomat under former President Barack Obama's administration, said the airport pomp delivered a propaganda win for Beijing. "Such extreme deference is valuable evidence that China's leader is now held in extraordinarily high esteem by the President of the United States. Beijing uses this at home and internationally to show China's — and Xi's — growing stature," said Russel, now at the Asia Society Policy Institute. China had hoped for a longer extension of the trade truce China had wanted a longer extension of the trade truce, which had been set to expire on Nov. 10. "It underscores that the United States is still concerned about China's full implementation of its commitments under the truce, particularly with respect to critical mineral exports and agricultural purchases," said Wendy Cutler, a former U.S. trade negotiator and now senior vice president at the Asia Society Policy Institute. The tight timeframe gives the U.S. a chance to test whether China will deliver on unmet promises to buy U.S. farm goods, said Craig Singleton, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies. "This is less about buying two months of calm than making China earn the next extension," he said. Trump has not yet commented on the extension. The two leaders are expected to talk about issues of substance more on Thursday, after an arrival ceremony at the White House and a review of troops. Later, they will exchange toasts at a black-tie dinner, which will feature tech industry leaders like Nvidia's Jensen Huang and SpaceX's Elon Musk. Trump to welcome Xi with 'the most respect' Trump has made it clear he wants to wow Xi, telling reporters in recent weeks that he was delighted his new "work of art" helicopter landing pad would be ready for the visit while bemoaning that his massive White House ballroom would not. "I wish we had it for tomorrow night," Trump said again Wednesday. Trump on Wednesday was looking to match the pageantry he was met with in China earlier this year. Xi was not at the airport to meet Trump — Chinese Vice President Han Zheng was there instead. But a red carpet was rolled out to meet Air Force One in Beijing. A military honor guard, a military band and about 300 Chinese youths waving Chinese and American flags and chanting, "Welcome, welcome! Warm welcome!" also were present. The first lady said earlier Wednesday that her husband decided to personally greet Xi when he arrived in the Washington region because "they have a great relationship." "He's coming on our soil, and we need to welcome them with the most respect," she said of Xi and his wife during an interview on Fox News Channel's "Fox & Friends." The long red carpet recalled a similar extra-long one the U.S. laid out for Russian President Vladimir Putin when he touched down at a U.S. Air Force base in Alaska last summer for a summit aimed at trying to find an end to Russia's war in Ukraine. On Friday, Xi and Peng will be back at the White House for a private tea with the Trumps before joining them on a tour of the National Archives in Washington. The White House has said they will view historic documents underscoring the relationship between the two countries. Associated Press writers Mary Clare Jalonick, Will Weissert and Collin Binkley contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. articles.title_orig: Pentagon investigates after China obtains parts from F-35 stealth fighter jet
articles.title_zh: Pentagon investigates after China obtains parts from F-35 stealth fighter jet
articles.content_orig:
The Department of Defence is examining how F-35 fighter jet parts bound for the US from Australia were unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong, the acting prime minister, Richard Marles, has said.
Marles said “very much everything that has occurred at the Australian end” would be reviewed, but claimed the technology parts were not “sensitive”, as first reported by Politico over the weekend.
The parts, which were being transported by another unknown third party on behalf of manufacturer, Lockheed Martin, still remain unaccounted for months later following their unplanned diversion to Hong Kong.
The last known location of the fighter jet components – in Hong Kong, a special administrative region of China – has sparked concern that some of the program’s technology secrets could have been exposed.
“We are examining [Australia’s involvement], but the point I would make here is that we are confident about the way in which we’ve engaged with the program, and through the US’s prime contractor, Lockheed,” Marles said on Tuesday.
“My understanding is that there is a sense of comfort, and we’re not talking about sensitive equipment here, or sensitive parts.
“Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred.”
Politico reported sources said the “sensitive” shipment contained one of the jet’s canopies, which reportedly contains stealth technology.
The US Department of War and F-35 Joint Program Office confirmed they were aware of the “shipment issue”.
“We are actively working with US authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence,” the spokesperson said.
While many details have not yet been revealed, Michael Shoebridge, a director for Strategic Analysis Australia who has worked in intelligence agencies, said there were two reasons why China, or another adversary, would want F-35 parts – to reverse engineer them, or to learn how to better exploit and attack them.
Shoebridge added the shipment’s pitstop in Hong Kong was “such an unexpectedly stupid thing” for the manufacturer or Australia to do.
“This is an act of incredible ineptitude and stupidity, and so it’s more the Chinese taking advantage of an incredible stroke of luck brought to them by the stupidity of the people involved,” he said.
Last week, the US State Department announced that the Trump administration would continue with the sale of 48 F-35s to Saudi Arabia, despite reported concerns from the US intelligence organisations that China could obtain some of the stealth technology.
Australia was one of the early development partners in the F-35. The program spreads the development, supply, management and sustainment of the fighter jets across different countries.
More than 70 Australian companies have production and sustainment contracts with the F-35 program. In excess of 700 of the fighter jet’s “critical pieces” are manufactured in Victoria alone, according to the state government. Australia also hosts a regional distribution hub for F-35 parts in New South Wales.
Australian companies involved in the program’s supply chain have been awarded contracts valued at over $5.2bn, as of September 2025.
Shoebridge said the missing shipment of parts could mean the whole multibillion-dollar fleet is vulnerable to adversaries.
“They’re all now carrying the risk of whatever vulnerabilities this has brought to the aircraft,” he said.
“So it’s not just a US-Australia issue. It’s every operator of the F-35 program [that] has an interest in understanding what happened and what was potentially exposed.”

articles.title_orig: US, China agree to extend trade truce by two months, work on bigger deal, Bessent says
articles.title_zh: US, China agree to extend trade truce by two months, work on bigger deal, Bessent says
articles.content_orig:
The United States and China have agreed to extend a bilateral trade truce that was set to expire in November through Jan. 10, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Wednesday.
The announcement came after Bessent and China’s vice premier, He Lifeng, held an unscheduled meeting in Washington.
“We will extend what we call the ‘Busan Agreement’ — the economic détente between the two countries that was scheduled to end on Nov. 10 — that is going to be extended until Jan. 10,” Bessent said in an interview on Fox News Channel.
Bessent said it’s possible a larger economic package will be agreed upon by January. But it’s also possible to “just roll the current deal” and extend it further.
“There are some deliverables that have not been perfect on the Chinese side, so we also want to see, now that we’ve sat down and told them our expectations, if over the coming months they can be more fulsome in enacting the agreement,” he said.
The announcement, a big win for economic stability in both countries, came only minutes after Chinese President Xi Jinping touched down to begin a multiday state visit to Washington.
Bessent also indicated that there could be further announcements in coming days from the Chinese delegation, including agreements to buy more American agricultural products and potential deals in the financial services sector.
Since Sunday, Bessent and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer have been holding talks with their Chinese counterparts to lay the groundwork for the closely watched state visit.
On Sunday, Bessent and Greer announced that the U.S. and China had proposed exchanging alerts about AI-related hacking incidents, especially those that concern national security.
The U.S. and China could also agree on lists of goods on which lower tariffs would be applied as part of President Donald Trump’s “Board of Trade” initiative with China, Greer told reporters.
“We expect that the types of goods you’ll see in those lists are consumer goods, low-tech items coming in from the Chinese side,” he said. “On the U.S. side, energy products, agricultural goods, potentially medical devices and other things like that.”
Xi’s visit is his first trip to the U.S. in more than a decade.
News of the trade truce extension is likely to be widely welcomed in Washington and Beijing, given that the U.S. and China are vital sources of goods for each other and for their millions of consumers and businesses.

articles.title_orig: Future of Air Force’s China Aerospace Studies Institute uncertain
articles.title_zh: Future of Air Force’s China Aerospace Studies Institute uncertain
articles.content_orig:
The Department of the Air Force is shutting down its premier think tank dedicated to studying Chinese aerospace, despite previously saying it would only cut civilian roles, according to the organization’s director.
On Tuesday, an Air Force spokesperson told Federal News Network that the service would no longer assign civilian positions to the China Aerospace Studies Institute as a part of the ongoing civilian restructure within Air Education and Training Command.
The spokesperson, however, did not confirm the assertion that CASI is shutting down, saying instead that the “mission continues with the organization leveraging assigned military service members to accomplish its objectives.”
“The China Aerospace Studies Institute is not closing,” the spokesperson said. “Air University continues to evaluate the alignment of the CASI mission to best support DAF priorities.”
“Civilian employees affected by this restructure will continue in their current positions until further notice and will be evaluated for reassignment,” the spokesperson added.
CASI’s official X account later published a statement that “Air University has decided to close the China Aerospace Studies Institute.”
Brendan Mulvaney, the organization’s director, said that all of CASI’s billets will go into an unfunded status beginning Oct. 1.
“That doesn’t mean we are going to cease operations right on the first of October. CASI has commitments that it has made and will honor, to the best of our ability, through at least March of 2027,” Mulvaney, who has been the center’s director since 2017, said in a statement.
“What it does mean is that the amazing team of researchers and scholars at CASI are going to have to start to look for new positions elsewhere. Rest assured, CASI employees will continue to work and get paid while in a ‘surplus’ status (meaning they remain employed and paid while we help them find new positions), and I will do my best to make sure they all land someplace that will truly appreciate their talents… As time goes on, unless we find a new home within the Department for the whole CASI team, I expect people to find other jobs and move on. Once all of the civilians eventually depart, CASI will close,” he added.
The Air Force spokesperson said that eight civilian positions have been impacted by the service’s 2026 civilian workforce optimization effort.
“Employees filling those positions will continue to serve and support CASI alongside five military members for the foreseeable future,” the spokesperson said.
CASI opened its doors in 2017 to study China’s air and space capabilities. The organization’s unclassified research informs policy and strategy across the Defense Department and broader U.S. government.
The defense community called the Air Force’s decision to “shutter” CASI “extremely unfortunate and regrettable,” describing the center as “the most prolific producer of publicly-accessible open source research about [the People’s Liberation Army] in the United States.”
“CASI has measurably increased knowledge about the PLA within the U.S. government, academia, think tanks and the broader public, which should be in the U.S. government’s interest, given that strategic competition with the PRC is the most important,” Will Yale, a Navy surface warfare officer, said on social media platform X.
Ryan Fedasiuk, a fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, said it is a “truly incomprehensible decision and a devastating loss for the analytic community.”
Workforce cuts at CASI are part of the Defense Department’s ongoing efforts to restructure its civilian workforce — the department eliminated approximately 78,000 civilian positions in 2025.
If you would like to contact this reporter about recent changes in the federal government, please email anastasia.obis@federalnewsnetwork.com or reach out on Signal at (301) 830-2747.
